Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45247")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45247")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

[LLM] Package manager runtime connecting to durabletask/axios supply-chain C2 IOCs Command & Control High
Network connections from node/python/npm/pip processes to the C2 IPs and domains attributed to the March 2026 axios npm hijack and May 2026 durabletask Python backdoor. Pivots on the article's exact infrastructure observables so it survives binary renaming and code refactors. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact C2 IPs (142.11.206.73, 160.119.64.3) and domains (sfrclak.com, check.git-service.com, t.m-kosche.com, packages.npm.org typosquat of packages.npmjs.org). Initiating process scoping to node/python/npm/pip turns this from a flat IOC sweep into a supply-chain-specific signal that distinguishes the malicious-package-postinstall pattern from a workstation browsing.

[LLM] Lateral movement via aws ssm send-command or kubectl exec spawned by python/node Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects the durabletask post-compromise tradecraft — backdoored Python (or its node equivalent) shelling out to aws/kubectl to spread laterally using the victim's own credentials via SSM SendCommand/StartSession or kubectl exec. The parent-runtime pivot is what makes this article-specific rather than a generic admin-tool detection. Rationale: The article specifies the durabletask backdoor spread 'to other instances over SSM and to other pods via kubectl exec' using the victim's own credentials. Filtering AWS/kubectl execution to a python/node parent makes this an actual supply-chain signal rather than admin-tool noise, and the CloudTrail variant catches the same activity by user-agent footprint when EDR isn't on the host.
ATT&CKT1021.007 T1609 T1078.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe","python","python3","node")
| where FileName in~ ("aws.exe","aws","kubectl.exe","kubectl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ssm send-command","ssm start-session","kubectl exec","exec -it","exec --stdin")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","python3","node","python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("aws","aws.exe","kubectl","kubectl.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ssm send-command","ssm start-session","kubectl exec","exec -it","exec --stdin")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c1d4b29-a6e8-4f93-bb12-2e8f5a90d147
status: experimental
description: Catches the durabletask post-compromise tradecraft where a backdoored Python (or node) interpreter shells out to aws/kubectl to move laterally via SSM SendCommand/StartSession or kubectl exec using the victim's own cloud credentials.
references:

logsource:

detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/python'

      - '/node'

      - '\node.exe'
  child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/aws'
      - '/kubectl'

    CommandLine|contains:

[LLM] Downloader or shell child of npm/pip install (postinstall RAT loader) Installation Medium
Detects the axios-style postinstall pattern where a malicious package's install hook reaches out for a second-stage payload via curl/wget/powershell/bitsadmin. The parent-equals-package-manager pivot turns generic downloader behavior into a supply-chain-specific signal. Rationale: The axios hijack 'added one new dependency whose only job was a postinstall script that pulled down a cross-platform RAT and deleted itself' — the loader behaviour is a download from a non-language-runtime binary spawned by the package manager. Parent==package-manager + child==downloader + URL/download-cmdline is the article's exact shape.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","npm","pip","pip3","yarn","pnpm")
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","bash","sh","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","Invoke-WebRequest","DownloadString","-OutFile","/dev/tcp/","base64 -d")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","pip","pip3","node","python","python3","yarn","pnpm")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","powershell","pwsh","bitsadmin","certutil","bash","sh")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","Invoke-WebRequest","DownloadString","-OutFile","/dev/tcp/","base64 -d")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Cloud credential file access by node/python runtime Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects the durabletask second-stage credential harvest where a backdoored Python (or node) runtime reads .aws/credentials, .azure, .kube/config, gcloud config, .vault-token, and .npmrc. Targets the file paths the article enumerates — AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Vault. Rationale: The article states the durabletask second stage 'harvested credentials from AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, and Vault'. The standard paths for those credential stores (~/.aws/credentials, ~/.kube/config, ~/.azure, ~/.config/gcloud, ~/.vault-token, ~/.npmrc) being touched by node/python is the concrete behaviour. The runtime filter keeps this from firing on AWS CLI / kubectl / az themselves.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node","python","python3")
| where FolderPath has_any (@".aws\credentials", ".aws/credentials", @".kube\config", ".kube/config", @".azure\", "/.azure/", "/.config/gcloud/", @"\gcloud\", ".vault-token", ".npmrc")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node","python","python3")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@".aws\credentials", ".aws/credentials", @".kube\config", ".kube/config", @".azure\", "/.azure/", "/.config/gcloud/", @"\gcloud\", ".vault-token", ".npmrc")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Cloud Credential File Access by Node/Python Runtime
id: 9b2f7e35-c1d4-4a86-b25f-3e7a1c8d0f49
status: experimental
description: Detects a Node.js or Python interpreter accessing AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes/Vault credential files — the durabletask backdoor second-stage harvest pattern.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/edr-proxy-wont-protect-supply-chain-malware
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/03
tags:
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.credential_access
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
  target:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\.aws\credentials'
      - '\.kube\config'
      - '\.azure\'
      - '\gcloud\'
      - '\.vault-token'
      - '\.npmrc'
  condition: proc and target
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\NODE.EXE OR *\python.exe OR *\PYTHON.EXE OR *\python3.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\.aws\credentials* OR *\.kube\config* OR *\.azure\* OR *\gcloud\* OR *\.vault-token* OR *\.npmrc*)) OR (source:linux.auditd @process.name:(node OR python OR python3) @auditd.type:PATH @file.path:(*/.aws/credentials* OR */.kube/config* OR */.azure/* OR */.config/gcloud/* OR */.vault-token* OR */.npmrc*))
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/(node|python3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("\\\\\\.aws\\\\credentials|/\\.aws/credentials|\\\\\\.kube\\\\config|/\\.kube/config|\\\\\\.azure\\\\|/\\.azure/|/\\.config/gcloud/|\\\\gcloud\\\\|\\.vault-token|\\.npmrc", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

[LLM] Locale-conditional rm -rf wiper command from python/node runtime Actions on Objectives High
Detects the durabletask wiper logic — a one-in-six destructive rm -rf /* invoked from a Python/Node interpreter on hosts with Israeli or Iranian locale. The rm -rf /* + python/node parent combination is the article's exact tradecraft. Rationale: The article states: 'On hosts with Israeli or Iranian locale settings, a one-in-six roll ran rm -rf /*'. The parent==python/node + cmdline==`rm -rf /*` combination is the literal article-specific impact behavior — extremely high signal because a developer never legitimately wipes their own root.
ATT&CKT1485 T1561.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe","python","python3","node")
| where FileName in~ ("rm","sh","bash","busybox","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\brm\s+-rf\s+(/\*?|--no-preserve-root)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","python3","node","python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\brm\s+-rf\s+(/\*?|--no-preserve-root)"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: rm -rf Wiper Spawned from Python/Node Runtime
id: 2a8d6e7f-93c1-4b50-8e2f-c47a9d1b35e0
status: experimental
description: Detects the durabletask backdoor wiper logic — a destructive rm -rf /* spawned from a Python or Node interpreter (one-in-six probability on hosts with Israeli/Iranian locale per the article).
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/edr-proxy-wont-protect-supply-chain-malware
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/03
tags:
  - attack.t1485
  - attack.t1561.001
  - attack.impact
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/node'
  cmdline:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'rm -rf /*'
      - 'rm -rf /'
      - 'rm -rf --no-preserve-root'
  condition: parent and cmdline
level: critical
(source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:("rm -rf /*" OR "rm -rf /" OR "rm -rf --no-preserve-root")) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:(*"rm -rf /*"* OR *"rm -rf /"* OR *"--no-preserve-root"*) @ParentImage:(*\python.exe OR *\python3.exe OR *\node.exe OR *\PYTHON.EXE OR *\NODE.EXE))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(python3?|node)(\.exe)?$/i ImageFileName=/^(rm|sh|bash|busybox|dash)$/i
| regex("\\brm\\s+-rf\\s+(/|--no-preserve-root)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "7d80b3ef74ad7992b93c31966962612e4e2ceb93e7727cdbd1d2a9af47d44ba8", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "aeaf583e20347bf850e2fabdcd6f4982996ba023f8c2cd56bbd299cfd56516f5", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "877ff2531a63393c4cb9a3c86908b62d9c4fc3db971bc231c48537faae6cb3ec", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-48595")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-48595")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Gamaredon Exploits WinRAR to Deliver GammaWorm and GammaSteel Against Ukraine

The Hacker News
2026-06-02 19 use cases 8 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

The Russian hacking group known as Gamaredon has been attributed to the continued exploitation of a WinRAR vulnerability to deliver multiple malware families aimed at data theft and propagation. Per Sekoia, the activity involves the weaponization of CVE-2025-8088, a path traversal flaw in WinRAR, to launch an HTML Application payload dubbed GammaPhish, which is then used to retrieve an

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 path traversal — file written from WinRAR into Startup folder · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GammaPhish HTA auto-execution — mshta.exe launching from user Startup folder · [LLM] GammaWorm NTFS Alternate Data Stream module hide — script-host writes file with ADS suffix · [LLM] GammaSteel registry-staged module fan-out — PowerShell writes many binary blobs under one key · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GammaWorm Telegram/Telegraph/Teletype/Cloudflare-Workers DDR resolution via curl from script host · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GammaWorm USB / network-share propagation — script process mass-creates LNK files on removable or remote drives · [LLM] GammaSteel S3 exfiltration — script/PowerShell HTTP egress to AWS S3 bucket · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 path traversal — file written from WinRAR into Startup folder Delivery High
Hunts the GammaPhish initial-access signature: a WinRAR / UnRAR / RAR process writes a file into a Windows Startup directory. CVE-2025-8088 lets a malicious archive traverse out of the chosen extraction path; Gamaredon weaponises it to drop an HTA dropper that auto-runs at next logon. Rationale: Article + Sekoia explicitly state the WinRAR exploit drops an HTA into the Startup directory via path traversal. Pairing the archive-tool image with the Startup destination is the cleanest single-event signature for CVE-2025-8088 exploitation. Cross-checked Sekoia blog and follow-on Hacker News CVE-2025-8088 coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/01/google-warns-of-active-exploitation-of.html • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/gamaredon-worm-ntfs-data-streams/
ATT&CKT1203 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe") | where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\" | where FileName !endswith ".log" and FileName !endswith ".tmp" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, ArchiveTool=InitiatingProcessFileName, ArchiveCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, DroppedFile=FileName, DropPath=FolderPath, SHA256 | order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where ActingProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe") | where TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256 | order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 Path Traversal Write Into Startup Folder
id: f1c5b3a2-9e7d-4b6a-b1f0-3d8c9e2a4711
description: WinRAR / UnRAR / RAR process writes a file directly into a Windows Startup directory — indicative of CVE-2025-8088 path-traversal exploitation used by Gamaredon to drop GammaPhish HTA.
references:
    - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/gamaredon-exploits-winrar-to-deliver.html
    - https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/02
tags:
    - attack.t1203
    - attack.t1547.001
    - attack.initial_access
    - attack.persistence
    - cve.2025.8088
logsource:
    category: file_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_proc:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\winrar.exe'
            - '\unrar.exe'
            - '\rar.exe'
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains: '\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\'
    condition: selection_proc and selection_path
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrator manually packaging Startup-folder shortcuts via WinRAR
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@Image:(*\\WinRAR.exe OR *\\winrar.exe OR *\\UnRAR.exe OR *\\unrar.exe OR *\\Rar.exe OR *\\rar.exe)) (@TargetFilename:(*\\Start\ Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\* OR *\\start\ menu\\programs\\startup\\*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/\\(winrar|unrar|rar)\.exe$/i TargetFileName=/\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name IN ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe","WinRAR.exe") OR Filesystem.process_path="*\\WinRAR\\*") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name IN ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe","WinRAR.exe") OR Filesystem.process_path="*\\WinRAR\\*") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
[LLM] GammaPhish HTA auto-execution — mshta.exe launching from user Startup folder Installation High
Hunts the GammaPhish auto-run: at next logon, explorer.exe launches mshta.exe against an HTA that CVE-2025-8088 dropped into the Startup folder. Pairing the parent (explorer) with the binary (mshta) and the HTA's path (Startup) is a high-fidelity catch for the post-exploit handoff to GammaLoad. Rationale: Sekoia and Hacker News articles describe the GammaPhish HTA being dropped directly into the Startup folder by the WinRAR exploit, which then auto-launches via mshta at logon. Combining explorer→mshta parentage with the Startup path eliminates the bulk of mshta noise from legitimate HTAs hosted elsewhere. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where FileName =~ "mshta.exe" | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe" | where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\" or ProcessCommandLine has_any (".hta",".HTA") and ProcessCommandLine has "Startup" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256 | order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where EventID == 4688 | where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe" | where ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe" | where CommandLine has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine | order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] GammaWorm Telegram/Telegraph/Teletype/Cloudflare-Workers DDR resolution via curl from script host Command & Control High
Hunts the GammaWorm dead-drop-resolver step: a VBScript host (wscript / cscript / mshta) spawns curl.exe to fetch a hardcoded public Telegram channel page (t.me/telegra.ph) or its Teletype.in / Cloudflare Workers fall-back, from which the actual C2 address is parsed. Catches the exact platform abuse Sekoia documents. Rationale: Sekoia's report explicitly names Telegram, Telegra.ph, Teletype.in, and Cloudflare Workers as Gamaredon's DDR platforms, and curl as the GammaWorm fetch tool. Pairing curl with a script-host parent and one of these four domains is single-event-shape and very rare in a legit corporate environment. One of the article IOCs (bold.zsjtn41091.workers.dev) is a Cloudflare Workers DDR endpoint. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where FileName =~ "curl.exe" | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe") | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("t.me/","telegra.ph","teletype.in",".workers.dev") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ScriptHost=InitiatingProcessFileName, ScriptCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, CurlCmd=ProcessCommandLine | order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where ActingProcessName endswith "curl.exe" | where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe") | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("t.me/","telegra.ph","teletype.in",".workers.dev") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine | order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] GammaWorm USB / network-share propagation — script process mass-creates LNK files on removable or remote drives Actions on Objectives High
Hunts GammaWorm's lateral-movement pattern: a VBScript host (wscript / cscript) writes many .lnk files to a removable drive or network share within a short window, while concurrently setting the hidden attribute on existing directories. The shortcut-replacing technique is Gamaredon's documented spread vector for USB and SMB. Rationale: Article specifies GammaWorm 'hide legitimate directories in network shares and USB drives and replace with malicious Windows Shortcut (LNK) files.' Detection keys on script-host parentage + drive letter outside C: or UNC root + LNK extension + burst count — none of these alone are unusual, but the combination is. Skipped Sigma because the threshold/grouping is multi-event correlation. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/
ATT&CKT1091 T1080 T1547.009

ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where EventType == "FileCreated" | where TargetFileName endswith ".lnk" | where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") | where TargetFilePath matches regex @"^(\\\\[^\\]+\\|[D-Z]:\\)" | summarize LnkCount=dcount(TargetFileName), Samples=make_set(TargetFileName, 5) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m) | where LnkCount >= 5

[LLM] GammaWorm NTFS Alternate Data Stream module hide — script-host writes file with ADS suffix Installation Medium
Hunts the GammaWorm defence-evasion technique: a VBScript host writes one of its core modules into an Alternate Data Stream (filename:streamname pattern) on a host file. Sekoia documents this as the primary on-disk hiding mechanism for the worm's modules. Rationale: Article + Infosecurity Magazine + Sekoia all confirm GammaWorm uses NTFS Alternate Data Streams to conceal its core modules. Script-host parentage + ADS-shape filename + Zone.Identifier exclusion is the cleanest single-event match. Cross-checked Infosecurity Magazine for technique confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/gamaredon-worm-ntfs-data-streams/ • https://undercodenews.com/silent-infiltration-russian-linked-gamaredon-worm-exploits-windows-hidden-streams-to-haunt-ukrainian-systems-without-a-trace-video/
ATT&CKT1564.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") | where FileName matches regex @"^[^:]+:[^:\\/]+$" | where FileName !endswith ":Zone.Identifier" and FileName !endswith ":SmartScreen" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, ScriptHost=InitiatingProcessFileName, ScriptCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ADSFile=FileName, ADSPath=FolderPath | order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") | where TargetFileName matches regex @"^[^:]+:[^:\\/]+$" | where TargetFileName !endswith ":Zone.Identifier" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath | order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] GammaSteel registry-staged module fan-out — PowerShell writes many binary blobs under one key Installation Medium
Hunts GammaSteel's documented self-staging behaviour: the PowerShell-based stealer writes ~71 DPAPI-encrypted modules as binary values into a single registry key, used as its in-memory loading store. The fan-out of binary registry values from a single PowerShell process to one parent key is article-specific and very rare. Rationale: Sekoia and follow-on coverage describe GammaSteel staging 71 encrypted PowerShell modules in the registry, protected by Windows DPAPI. Threshold ≥20 distinct binary values under one HKCU/HKLM\Software key written by a single PowerShell/wscript process in 30 minutes catches the staging without over-firing on legitimate per-value config writes. Multi-event correlation, so Sigma is intentionally skipped. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/
ATT&CKT1112 T1140 T1055.012
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
DeviceRegistryEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueModified") | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") | where RegistryValueType in ("Binary","None") | where RegistryKey startswith @"HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\" or RegistryKey startswith @"HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\" | summarize DistinctValues=dcount(RegistryValueName), TotalWrites=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Sample=any(RegistryValueData) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RegistryKey, bin(Timestamp, 30m) | where DistinctValues >= 20 | order by DistinctValues desc
ImRegistryEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where EventType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueModified") | where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") | where RegistryValueType in ("Binary","REG_BINARY") | summarize DistinctValues=dcount(RegistryValue), TotalWrites=count() by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m) | where DistinctValues >= 20
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\WScript.exe)) (@TargetObject:(*\\Software\\* OR *\\SOFTWARE\\*))
#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate ContextImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i | regex("\\\\Software\\\\", field=RegObjectName, flags=i) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RegObjectName], function={distinct_values := count(field=RegValueName, distinct=true) | total := count()}) | distinct_values >= 20
ENDPOINT

[LLM] GammaSteel S3 exfiltration — script/PowerShell HTTP egress to AWS S3 bucket Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the GammaSteel exfiltration path: a script host or PowerShell process not normally seen on the wire issues an outbound HTTPS connection to *.s3.amazonaws.com (or s3.<region>.amazonaws.com) to upload harvested files. Article specifies S3 as the primary exfil with attacker-controlled web servers as a fallback. Rationale: Article explicitly names AWS S3 as GammaSteel's exfil destination with attacker-controlled fallback. The hunt isolates the unusual combination of script-host parentage and S3 egress — neither AWSPowerShell nor aws-cli are in the included process list, so legitimate S3 backup activity from a developer workstation falls outside scope. Tier set to hunting because S3 is widely used; analyst should pivot from any hit to the parent process chain. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0d
status: experimental
description: |
    schtasks.exe /create with payload-shaped action — points at
    powershell, cmd, rundll32, encoded-base64, or user-writable paths.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1053.005
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_schtasks:
        Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: '/create'
    selection_payload:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'powershell'
            - 'cmd.exe'
            - 'rundll32'
            - '-enc'
            - 'FromBase64'
            - '\Users\Public'
            - '\AppData\'
    condition: selection_schtasks and selection_payload
falsepositives:
    - GPO-driven scheduled tasks, MDT/SCCM imaging
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows

    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'

            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'

let BadHashes = dynamic(["b2ba51b4491da8604ff9410d6e004971e3cd9a321390d0258e294ac42010b546", "1ed863a32372160b3a25549aad25d48d5352d9b4f58d4339408c4eea69807f50", "5a17cfaea0cc3a82242fdd11b53140c0b56256d769b07c33757d61e0a0a6ec02", "fd3f13db41cd5b442fa26ba8bc0e9703ed243b3516374e3ef89be71cbf07436b", "c91183175ce77360006f964841eb4048cf37cb82103f2573e262927be4c7607f", "a944a09783023a2c6c62d3601cbd5392a03d808a6a51728e07a3270861c2a8ee", "bb23545380fde9f48ad070f88fe0afd695da5fcae8c5274814858c5a681d8c4e", "0bb0d54033767f081cae775e3cf9ede7ae6bea75f35fbfb748ccba9325e28e5e", "a876f648991711e44a8dcf888a271880c6c930e5138f284cd6ca6128eca56ba1", "2822c72a59b58c00fc088aa551cdeeb92ca10fd23e23745610ff207f53118db9", "9f4672c1374034ac4556264f0d4bf96ee242c0b5a9edaa4715b5e61fe8d55cc8", "3f446d316efe2514efd70c975d0c87e12357db9fca54a25834d60b28192c6a69", "1794369214b7f62e70a0485e61335c61", "8e1624d110c090ff57d4b493a9107c66"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] npm/node lifecycle script fetching Bun runtime from github.com/oven-sh/bun Installation High
Detects an npm preinstall/postinstall lifecycle script (node.exe parented by npm) reaching out to github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases to download the Bun v1.3.13 runtime. This is the exact bootstrap behaviour of the TeamPCP @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 payload (bw_setup.js Stage-1) and is highly anomalous on developer endpoints because legitimate JS projects rarely pull Bun via a package-install hook. Rationale: Article explicitly names github.com/oven-sh/bun and Bun v1.3.13 as the runtime downloaded by Stage-1 bw_setup.js during npm preinstall — pairing the github.com/oven-sh/bun URL token with an npm-family parent process is a near-zero-FP signature on production endpoints (developer laptops will produce occasional FPs, hence the parent-process pinning). Cross-checked against Socket and Checkmarx advisories listed below. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/teampcp-bitwarden-cli-supply-chain • https://checkmarx.com/blog/checkmarx-supply-chain-incident-april-2026/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
let bunUrlIndicators = dynamic(["github.com/oven-sh/bun", "oven-sh/bun/releases", "bun-windows-x64", "bun-linux-x64", "bun-darwin"]);
let npmParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","npm-cli.js","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe"]);
let downloaderChildren = dynamic(["node.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","wget.exe","bun.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","pwsh.exe"]);
// Process-tree pivot — npm parent spawning a downloader child with Bun URL on the command line
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (npmParents) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (npmParents)
    | where FileName in~ (downloaderChildren)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (bunUrlIndicators) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (bunUrlIndicators)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
              ParentImage = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
              InitImage  = InitiatingProcessFileName,
              InitCmd    = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              ChildImage = FileName,
              ChildCmd   = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
// Network pivot — same process families connecting to github.com for the Bun release tarball
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where RemoteUrl has "github.com" and (RemoteUrl has "oven-sh/bun" or RemoteUrl has "bun-windows" or RemoteUrl has "bun-linux" or RemoteUrl has "bun-darwin")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (downloaderChildren)
    | where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (npmParents) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (npmParents)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName,
              AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              ParentImage = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
              InitImage   = InitiatingProcessFileName,
              InitCmd     = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              ChildImage  = "<network-egress>", ChildCmd = RemoteUrl, SHA256 = InitiatingProcessSHA256;
union ProcHits, NetHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let bunUrlIndicators = dynamic(["github.com/oven-sh/bun", "oven-sh/bun/releases", "bun-windows-x64", "bun-linux-x64", "bun-darwin"]);
let npmParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","npm-cli.js","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe","npm","node","yarn","pnpm","npx"]);
let downloaderChildren = dynamic(["node.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","wget.exe","bun.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","pwsh.exe","node","curl","wget","bun","bash","sh","pwsh"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any (downloaderChildren) or ParentProcessName has_any (downloaderChildren)
| where (ParentProcessName has_any (npmParents) or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (npmParents) or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (npmParents))
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (bunUrlIndicators) or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (bunUrlIndicators)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: NPM Lifecycle Script Downloading Bun Runtime from oven-sh GitHub
id: 4c2f6f8a-9d1e-4b8c-9a3f-2e8a0b1c4d51
status: experimental
description: Detects an npm/yarn/pnpm install lifecycle script (Node.js parented by npm) spawning a downloader to fetch the Bun JavaScript runtime from github.com/oven-sh/bun — the Stage-1 bootstrap of the TeamPCP @bitwarden/cli supply-chain payload.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/monitoring-npm-supply-chain-attacks/
  - https://socket.dev/blog/teampcp-bitwarden-cli-supply-chain
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/20
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
      - '\npx.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
      - '\bun.exe'
  selection_url:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'github.com/oven-sh/bun'
      - 'oven-sh/bun/releases'
      - 'bun-windows-x64'
      - 'bun-linux-x64'
      - 'bun-darwin'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_url
falsepositives:
  - Developer manually upgrading the Bun runtime via an automation script
  - CI agent installing Bun in a build pipeline (scope detection to dev workstations or scope out CI hosts)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\npm.exe OR *\NPM.exe OR *\node.exe OR *\NODE.exe OR *\yarn.exe OR *\pnpm.exe OR *\npx.exe) @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\NODE.exe OR *\curl.exe OR *\CURL.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\wget.exe OR *\bun.exe) @CommandLine:(*github.com/oven-sh/bun* OR *oven-sh/bun/releases* OR *bun-windows-x64* OR *bun-linux-x64* OR *bun-darwin*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(npm|node|yarn|pnpm|npx)(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(node|curl|powershell|pwsh|wget|bun|bash|sh)\.exe$/i
| regex("github\.com/oven-sh/bun|oven-sh/bun/releases|bun-(windows|linux|darwin)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

[LLM] C2 beacon to audit.checkmarx[.]cx /v1/telemetry (TeamPCP Shai-Hulud Third Coming) Command & Control High
Detects any outbound network/DNS activity to the TeamPCP C2 audit.checkmarx[.]cx (94.154.172.43) — particularly POSTs to the /v1/telemetry path — that exfiltrates harvested cloud, CI/CD and developer credentials from compromised hosts. The domain visually impersonates Checkmarx's legitimate infrastructure but resolves to attacker-controlled space. Rationale: Article Table 1 names the C2 server, IP and HTTP path explicitly (audit.checkmarx[.]cx:443 / 94.154.172.43 / /v1/telemetry) — any hit on these three indicators is a confirmed-compromise signal, not a hunting hypothesis. Corroborated by Checkmarx's official disclosure that all four artifact families (npm, Docker Hub, GitHub Actions, VS Code) shared this C2. Cross-checked against: • https://checkmarx.com/blog/checkmarx-supply-chain-incident-april-2026/ • https://socket.dev/blog/teampcp-bitwarden-cli-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
let c2Hosts = dynamic(["audit.checkmarx.cx", "audit.checkmarx[.]cx"]);
let c2Ips    = dynamic(["94.154.172.43"]);
let c2Path   = "/v1/telemetry";
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteUrl has_any (c2Hosts)) or (RemoteIP in (c2Ips)) or (RemoteUrl has c2Path and RemotePort in (443, 80))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2Hosts = dynamic(["audit.checkmarx.cx"]);
let c2Ips    = dynamic(["94.154.172.43"]);
let c2Path   = "/v1/telemetry";
union isfuzzy=true
(
  ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstHostname has_any (c2Hosts) or DstIpAddr in (c2Ips) or (isnotempty(Url) and Url has c2Path and DstPortNumber in (443, 80))
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
),
(
  ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has_any (c2Hosts)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsQueryTypeName, DnsResponseCodeName
),
(
  ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where HttpHostName has_any (c2Hosts) or Url has c2Path and (HttpHostName has "checkmarx.cx")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode
),
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationHostName has_any (c2Hosts) or DestinationIP in (c2Ips) or RequestURL has "audit.checkmarx.cx" or RequestURL has c2Path
  | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TeamPCP Shai-Hulud C2 audit.checkmarx[.]cx Connection
id: 7e5a3b2c-1f4d-4a6e-9b8f-3c2d1e4f5a62
status: experimental
description: Detects connections or DNS resolutions to the TeamPCP / Shai-Hulud Third Coming C2 infrastructure (audit.checkmarx[.]cx / 94.154.172.43) used by the @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 npm supply-chain payload and the broader Checkmarx-distribution-channel compromise to exfiltrate harvested credentials via /v1/telemetry.
references:

[LLM] Malicious @bitwarden/cli payload artifacts on disk (bw_setup.js, bw1.js, Shai-Hulud markers) Installation High
Detects creation or execution of the Stage-1 (bw_setup.js) and Stage-2 (bw1.js) Node.js scripts dropped by the TeamPCP @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 npm package, as well as the 'Shai-Hulud: The Third Coming' string written into public repo content that the worm uses as an attribution marker and propagation beacon. This catches both the install-time drop on the npm install path and any post-compromise replay. Rationale: Article explicitly names bw_setup.js (Stage-1 bootstrap, registered as the `bw` bin) and bw1.js (Stage-2 Bun payload) inside the malicious @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 package. The legitimate Bitwarden CLI ships neither filename, so the filename + package path combo is a hard-IOC match. The Shai-Hulud Third Coming string is a TeamPCP attribution marker per the article body. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/teampcp-bitwarden-cli-supply-chain • https://github.com/bitwarden/clients/security/advisories
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546.016 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
let stageFiles = dynamic(["bw_setup.js", "bw1.js"]);
let packageHints = dynamic(["@bitwarden\\cli", "@bitwarden/cli", "node_modules\\@bitwarden\\cli", "node_modules/@bitwarden/cli"]);
let shaiHuludMarker = "Shai-Hulud: The Third Coming";
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where (FileName in~ (stageFiles)) or (FolderPath has_any (packageHints) and FileName endswith ".js") or (AdditionalFields has shaiHuludMarker)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName,
              AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
              FolderPath, FileName, SHA256;
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npm-cli.js","bun.exe")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (stageFiles)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
              FolderPath, FileName = FileName, SHA256, ProcCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
union FileHits, ProcHits
| order by Timestamp desc

let npmRunners = dynamic(["npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npm-cli.js","bun.exe","npm","node","yarn","pnpm","bun"]);
let FileHits = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
